items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: when I played eventually played with Alice Coltrane... Alice Coltrane showed me that bass line. 'This is what I want you to play.'

ctx.x: Well that bass line, there’s a tingling in my brain. It reminds me of something. Was that Alice Coltrane?
That’s correct. I’m not sure I can pronounce the title correctly, “Journey to Satchidananda.”

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: I don’t know if you can compare your experience to someone else, but you played from ’69 to ’72 if my facts are correct, both with Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders simultaneously? ... Mostly with Pharoah. I was in Pharoah’s band at the time. Occasionally I’d play a concert with Alice.

ctx.x: Well I want to get back to that in a while because that sounds really uplifting. I wanted to make a few stops in your life that you had talked about two weeks ago, and first of all a brief question about your upbringing in Oklahoma. You said that the social conditions there were difficult when you were a child and I wonder if you could expand on that.

Well I was raised by my single parent mother. And there were three brothers and two sisters, right? I was number three in the rotation if you will. And I truly, you know, given recent news about Tulsa, Oklahoma, about conditions that took place during the race riots, okay? My mother had, all these years, had related to us that at eight years of age she had to drop out of school because of the loss of both parents in the same year. This was in © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Southern Texas. And so she and her three sisters, elder sisters, she was the youngest of thirteen kids. They moved to Tulsa, and my mother, Alice, was the only one that had children which was of course us. And she — God I hate to say this — it’s very uncomfortable to say this but I never looked at my father in his eyes and said hello. Or who are you or what is this about. He was nowhere to be found. I think my older brothers, they knew him. They never talked about it. She never talked about it. And so she, when I…

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: there was a lady whose name was Alice McLeod. She would have jam sessions at her big Victorian home every Sunday, which I would, you know, participate in occasionally.

ctx.x: Louis Hayes. I was sort of a, until now, an adopted son of Detroit, because people seem to have liked what I did. And so I got a chance to play with everybody. And you learn that, you know, at that particular time Detroit was the place where most of the great musicians, you know, came from, you know, Barry Harris, and — there was a vibe there, there was a lady whose name was Alice McLeod. She would have jam sessions at her big Victorian home every Sunday, which I would, you know, participate in occasionally.…

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: INTERVIEWER: ...we made note of jam sessions at Alice McLeod’s residence. This is the future Alice Coltrane is that right? INTERVIEWEE: Exactly.

ctx.x: Yeah. Can you describe for us what that was like? What would the tunes be? And was the function of it partly to meet people, to maybe find gigs and just improve yourself?

No. The function of it, mind you I’m the young guy. I’m just there you know. I’m out of the exterior if you will. The function of it was to touch base. The musicians that would gather there each and every Sunday that might be in town or might be at home, but just meet and have a good time playing music. So what? It wasn’t about having a gig or anything like that. Because as I mentioned before on the way to New York, now that I’m out of the Army where I practiced my bass every night until three or four in the…
Did you join the military or were you drafted?
